```{r mdomain-setup, include=FALSE}
have_gmp <- requireNamespace("gmp", quietly = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = have_gmp, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 120, out.width = "100%")
options(width = 82)
```

Whereas `postrank()` assigns one common grade shared across criteria, a
multidomain report card assigns each unit a **separate integer grade in each
domain**. A unit can receive higher priority in one domain and lower priority in
another. Within each domain, Grade 1 is the highest priority, and giving two
units the same grade leaves that pair unordered in that domain without claiming
that their underlying targets are equal. As throughout `postrank`, statistical
model fitting happens outside the package and results depend on the posterior
you supply.

This article builds a two-state discrete probability distribution for three
units across two domains, evaluates a proposed multidomain report card, searches
a declared set of candidate grade columns, plots three views of the selected
card, and compares exact, IID, and MCMC assessment modes. All calculations run
offline without an external MIP or LP solver when the suggested `gmp` package
(used for exact rational arithmetic) is installed via `install.packages("gmp")`.

```{r mdomain-load, eval=TRUE}
library(postrank)
```

```{r mdomain-dependency-note, echo=FALSE, results='asis', eval=TRUE}
if (!have_gmp) cat("**Computation skipped:** the optional package `gmp` is not installed. Install `gmp` and rebuild to run the examples.\n")
```

The multidomain workflow uses eight functions:

| Function | Role |
|:--|:--|
| `postrank_mdomain_input()` | Attach joint or domain-wise states to target definitions and source metadata. |
| `postrank_mdomain_decision()` | Set domain loss weights, withholding costs, expected-error budgets, and joint exceedance caps. |
| `postrank_mdomain_evaluate()` | Evaluate a fixed unit-by-domain integer grade matrix. |
| `postrank_mdomain_grades()` | Extract the verified grade matrix from an evaluated card or solved fit. |
| `postrank_mdomain_family()` | Declare the candidate grade columns allowed in each domain. |
| `postrank_mdomain_solve()` | Evaluate every combination in the declared candidate set and select an optimal feasible card. |
| `postrank_mdomain_assess()` | Check joint-exceedance quantities under `"exact"`, `"iid"`, or `"mcmc"` rules. |
| `postrank_plot_mdomain()` | Plot domain grades (`"grades"`), profile cells (`"cells"`), or two-unit comparisons (`"pair"`). |

## Building a multidomain input from joint states

Joint state arrays have dimensions **`state x unit x domain`**, where each state
slice holds all units and all domains together so cross-unit and cross-domain
dependence are preserved. Below, two slices specify a complete discrete
posterior—putting probability `9/10` on `"usual"` and `1/10` on `"reversal"`
rather than approximating a continuous distribution with two Monte Carlo draws:

```{r mdomain-states}
unit_ids <- c("Alder", "Birch", "Cedar")
domain_ids <- c("attainment", "community")
states <- array(NA_real_, c(2L, 3L, 2L),
  dimnames = list(c("usual", "reversal"), unit_ids, domain_ids))
states["usual", , "attainment"] <- c(3, 2, 1)
states["usual", , "community"] <- c(2, 3, 1)
states["reversal", , "attainment"] <- c(2, 3, 1)
states["reversal", , "community"] <- c(3, 2, 1)
```

Every domain must already be oriented so that larger values mean higher
priority (`orientation = "larger_is_higher"`). In each domain's target record,
`equality_classes` declares structural model identities across units: giving
each unit its own class label states that the model does not force two units to
share an identical target (even if two units happen to tie in an individual
state):

```{r mdomain-targets}
targets <- setNames(lapply(domain_ids, function(d) list(
  definition = paste("Fictional", d, "priority coordinate"),
  units = "illustrative score", orientation = "larger_is_higher",
  transformations = list(),
  equality_classes = setNames(unit_ids, unit_ids),
  equality_provenance = "The model imposes no identity between distinct units."
)), domain_ids)
```

Next we describe where the distribution came from (`provenance`) and combine the
states, target definitions, and exact rational state probabilities (`masses`) in
`postrank_mdomain_input()`:

```{r mdomain-provenance}
provenance <- list(
  input_id = "three-unit-support", law_id = "fictional-two-state-law",
  proper_law = TRUE, producer = "Self-contained teaching example",
  conditioning_info = "No observations: this is a specified probability law.",
  joint_generation = paste("Each labeled slice is one complete state",
    "of all units and domains."),
  sampling_assumptions = list(finite_support_origin = paste(
    "These two states exhaust the specified fictional law;",
    "they are not sampled draws."))
)
```

```{r mdomain-input}
input <- postrank_mdomain_input(states, targets = targets,
  provenance = provenance, representation = "exact_finite_law",
  masses = c("9/10", "1/10"))
input
```

`postrank_mdomain_input()` checks array dimensions, ID ordering, probability
masses, and required metadata fields; it does not verify that an upstream model
is well specified or properly sampled. Keep the same unit order and domain order
across `targets`, policy vectors, and grade matrices (and never pair separate
domain simulations by row number as if they came from a joint state).

## Choosing a decision rule and evaluating a profile card

Our policy gives equal weight (`"1/2"` and `"1/2"`) to the two domains, charges
`tau = "1/5"` per unordered pair, omits per-domain expected-error budgets
(`q = NULL`), and bounds the **joint** exceedance probability across domains by
`alpha = "1/5"` at error-proportion threshold `t = "0"` (at `t = "0"`, a single
wrong-direction ordered pair in either domain triggers the exceedance event):

```{r mdomain-fixed-card}
decision <- postrank_mdomain_decision(
  weights = c(attainment = "1/2", community = "1/2"),
  tau = "1/5", q = NULL, t = "0", alpha = "1/5")

G <- cbind(attainment = c(1, 2, 3), community = c(2, 1, 3))
rownames(G) <- unit_ids
card <- postrank_mdomain_evaluate(input, G, decision)
card
postrank_mdomain_grades(card)
```

Notice that `Alder` has profile `(1, 2)` while `Birch` has `(2, 1)`: `Alder`
ranks higher in `attainment` and `Birch` ranks higher in `community`, with no
single combined ranking forced onto the two units. Under the supplied finite
distribution, this card has exact additive loss `1/30` (`risk_exact`) and exact
joint exceedance probability `1/10` (`J_exact`), satisfying `alpha = "1/5"`
because the `"reversal"` state causes wrong-direction orders in both domains
simultaneously and is counted once in the union event:

```{r mdomain-tables}
card[["domain_table"]][, c("domain_id", "N", "EF_exact", "loss_exact")]
card[["event_table"]][, c("domain_id", "N", "cutoff_exact", "p_exact")]
card[["feasible_for_represented_measure"]]
```

With three units, every domain has `M = choose(3, 2) = 3` unordered pairs. Domain
loss divides expected wrong-direction pairs plus `tau` times unordered pairs by
`M`, whereas the protected error proportion divides wrong-direction pairs `F` by
`N`, the number of ordered (`disclosed`) pairs in that scope—triggering when
`F / N > t` (that is, `F >= floor(t * N) + 1`). Ordering two units strictly when
their targets are equal counts as a wrong-direction error. Within each domain,
units sharing that domain's `equality_classes` label must receive the same
grade, even when the domain has weight zero. Two units can therefore share an
attainment grade and receive different community grades if the community model
assigns them to distinct classes.

When a column leaves all pairs unordered (`N = 0`), the error proportion `eFDP`
is `NA`, the zero-when-withheld convention `eFDP_zero` is `0` (with
`eFDP_zero_exact` equal to `"0"`), and `F / N > t` cannot occur in any state
(which is structural, distinct from observing zero exceedances in a small Monte
Carlo sample):

```{r mdomain-withholding}
withheld <- postrank_mdomain_evaluate(input, G * 0 + 1, decision)
withheld[["scope_table"]][, c("domain_id", "N", "eFDP", "eFDP_zero")]
withheld[["status"]][["joint"]]
```

Pass exact fractions or decimal strings (such as `"1/10"` or `"0.1"`) in
`postrank_mdomain_decision()` whenever a policy threshold is an exact rational
number; a bare R numeric literal such as `0.1` keeps its binary floating-point
value, which can differ at strict inequality boundaries. Integer grade labels
only encode order and shared grades and are relabeled to `1, 2, ...` (`10, 20, 30`
defines the exact same card as `1, 2, 3`).

## Searching a declared set of candidate columns

`postrank_mdomain_family()` lists the grade columns allowed in each domain in
original unit order (always including the 1-grade all-withheld column). With two
allowed columns in each of two domains, the Cartesian product contains four
candidate report cards, and `postrank_mdomain_solve()` evaluates all four:

```{r mdomain-search}
family <- postrank_mdomain_family(input, columns = list(
  attainment = list(setNames(G[, "attainment"], unit_ids)),
  community = list(setNames(G[, "community"], unit_ids))),
  max_actions = 4L)
fit <- postrank_mdomain_solve(input, family, decision, max_actions = 4L)
fit
fit[["candidate_table"]][, c("risk_exact", "J_exact",
  "feasible_for_represented_measure", "optimal", "selected")]
postrank_mdomain_grades(fit)
```

Among these four candidates, the crossing card (`risk_exact = "1/30"`,
`J_exact = "1/10"`) achieves the smallest loss while meeting the joint
exceedance cap. **Optimality holds only within the declared candidate set:**
`postrank_mdomain_solve()` makes no claim about grade partitions outside
`family`. When multiple candidates tie at the minimum exact loss, all tied
optimizers are flagged (`optimal = TRUE`) and the first in lexicographic order
of the renumbered (`1..K_d`) grade columns is marked `selected = TRUE`. The
`max_actions` cap stops with an error before enumerating an oversized Cartesian
product rather than truncating the search.

To build larger ordered candidate sets per domain, pass unit-ID permutations to
`order` and allowed cutpoints to `cuts` in `postrank_mdomain_family()`. Choosing
`order = "posterior_mean"` computes each domain's ordering from the supplied
states and records that data-dependent choice in metadata (which is not an
independent held-out validation).

## Plotting three views of a multidomain card

`postrank_plot_mdomain()` renders three views from the stored card or solved fit
without running new evaluations. Setting `domain_labels` or `unit_labels`
relabels axes for display while keeping underlying IDs intact:

```{r mdomain-grades-view, fig.cap="Multidomain grade profiles for Alder, Birch, and Cedar across Attainment and Community; Alder is Grade 1 in Attainment and Grade 2 in Community, whereas Birch reverses those two grades.", fig.alt="Two-column grade plot for Alder, Birch, and Cedar across Attainment and Community showing crossed first and second grades for Alder and Birch and Grade 3 for Cedar."}
postrank_plot_mdomain(fit, view = "grades",
  domain_labels = c(attainment = "Attainment", community = "Community"))
```

`view = "cells"` counts how many units fall in each `(attainment, community)`
grade combination while keeping empty cells visible (profile cells are a
two-dimensional grid rather than a single combined ranking):

```{r mdomain-cells-view, fig.cap="Occupied and empty profile cells across the three Attainment grades and three Community grades, with one unit each at (1, 2), (2, 1), and (3, 3).", fig.alt="Three-by-three grid of Attainment-by-Community grade cells showing count 1 at (1, 2), (2, 1), and (3, 3) and count 0 elsewhere."}
postrank_plot_mdomain(fit, view = "cells")
```

`view = "pair"` compares two selected units across every domain (`units` filters
only what is drawn, while caption losses and exceedance probabilities still
describe the full report card):

```{r mdomain-pair-view, fig.cap="Pairwise domain comparison between Alder and Birch: Alder has higher reported priority in attainment and Birch has higher reported priority in community.", fig.alt="Two-domain comparison diagram showing Alder ahead of Birch in attainment and Birch ahead of Alder in community."}
postrank_plot_mdomain(fit, view = "pair", units = c("Alder", "Birch"))
```

## Using posterior draws and choosing `"exact"`, `"iid"`, or `"mcmc"` assessment

When your posterior comes from Monte Carlo simulation rather than a closed
finite distribution, keep all units and domains from each draw together in one
slice with unique draw IDs (you can also pass an existing validated
`postrank_draws` object directly to `postrank_mdomain_input()` with
`provenance = list(input_id = ..., law_id = ..., proper_law = TRUE)`, leaving
`targets = NULL` so its stored target definitions and sampling metadata carry
over). Below we draw `20` independent states from the two-state distribution:

```{r mdomain-iid-draws}
set.seed(120)
draw_rows <- sample.int(2L, 20L, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.9, 0.1))
joint_draws <- states[draw_rows, , , drop = FALSE]
dimnames(joint_draws)[[1L]] <- paste0("draw-", seq_len(20L))
draw_provenance <- provenance
draw_provenance[["input_id"]] <- "three-unit-iid-draws"
draw_provenance[["joint_generation"]] <- "Independent draws of complete two-domain states."
draw_provenance[["sampling_assumptions"]] <- list(
  iid_mechanism = "Independent categorical draws from the two-state law.",
  target_assertion = "Each complete draw targets fictional-two-state-law."
)
```

```{r mdomain-iid-eval}
draw_input <- postrank_mdomain_input(joint_draws, targets = targets,
  provenance = draw_provenance, representation = "iid_equal_weight_draws")
draw_card <- postrank_mdomain_evaluate(draw_input, G, decision)
draw_card[["assurance"]][c("numerical_basis",
  "intended_posterior_feasibility_certified")]
```

**Exact rational arithmetic (`gmp`) over empirical draw counts or a finite
distribution is not a numerical guarantee about the intended posterior**
(`intended_posterior_feasibility_certified` is `FALSE`). Match
`postrank_mdomain_assess()` to how your states were produced:

- **`method = "iid"`**: evaluates a fixed-sample binomial tail check when the
  grade matrix, decision policy, target law, sample size, and failure budget
  were fixed *before* drawing independent validation states (reusing states that
  selected or ordered the card does not satisfy that design).
- **`method = "mcmc"`**: requires `representation = "mcmc_equal_weight_draws"`
  with `state_origin` (`source_index`, `chain_id`, `iteration_id` in supplied
  state order) and computes descriptive chain and batch summaries; zero observed
  exceedances and chain summaries do not provide an IID guarantee or prove
  convergence.
- **`method = "exact"`**: evaluates the exact joint-exceedance probability under
  a complete `exact_finite_law` (describing that finite distribution without
  checking model calibration, expected-error budgets `q`, or optimality):

```{r mdomain-assessment}
assessed <- postrank_mdomain_assess(input, fit, method = "exact")
assessed
assessed[["certificate_scope"]]
```

See
[Separate domain rules versus joint multidomain protection](mdomain-decisions.html)
for cross-domain dependence examples and MCMC chain diagnostics.

## Fixing two common input mistakes

Multidomain validation errors inherit class `"postrank_mdomain_error"` and store
machine-readable `code` and `field` entries so scripts can inspect what failed
without parsing error text. First, omitting `joint_generation` on a 3D state
array stops on `provenance.joint_generation`:

```{r mdomain-missing-joint}
incomplete <- provenance
incomplete[["joint_generation"]] <- NULL
missing_joint <- tryCatch(
  postrank_mdomain_input(states, targets = targets, provenance = incomplete,
    representation = "exact_finite_law", masses = c("9/10", "1/10")),
  postrank_mdomain_error = identity)
c(code = missing_joint[["code"]], field = missing_joint[["field"]])
```

Supply your actual `joint_generation` statement when states come from one joint
distribution, or pass a domain-named list of 2D `state x unit` matrices with
`within_domain_joint` in `provenance` when domains come from separate fits
(never claim joint generation just because separate fits have the same number of
rows).

Second, passing a grade matrix whose row order differs from `input$unit_ids`
stops on `grades`:

```{r mdomain-reordered-grades}
reordered <- G[c("Birch", "Alder", "Cedar"), , drop = FALSE]
bad_ids <- tryCatch(postrank_mdomain_evaluate(input, reordered, decision),
  postrank_mdomain_error = identity)
c(code = bad_ids[["code"]], field = bad_ids[["field"]])

repaired <- reordered[input[["unit_ids"]], input[["domain_ids"]], drop = FALSE]
postrank_mdomain_grades(postrank_mdomain_evaluate(input, repaired, decision))
```

Reorder rows and columns by name (`[input$unit_ids, input$domain_ids, drop = FALSE]`)
rather than overwriting `rownames()` or `colnames()`, which would attach grades
to the wrong units.
